seoTitle: Free Crockford Base32 Encoder and Decoder
metaDescription: Encode text or hex bytes to Crockford Base32, which skips I, L, O and U and reads O and I as 0 and 1. Free, runs in your browser.
intro: Encode text or hex bytes to Crockford Base32, or decode it back. The alphabet avoids easily confused letters and is case-insensitive when decoding.
why:
Douglas Crockford designed his Base32 to be read and typed by people. It leaves out I, L, O and U so that you do not confuse them with 1 and 0, and to avoid accidental rude words. Decoders treat O as zero and I or L as one, and ignore hyphens, so a value copied from a printout still decodes.

You will see it in ULIDs, which use the same alphabet for their 26-character form, and in some human-friendly identifiers. This tool lets you encode bytes or text, or decode a string to see what it holds. Note that it is the plain alphabet with no check symbol, and it is not RFC 4648 Base32.
howTo: Choose encode or decode, and whether the bytes are text or hex.
Paste your input. Hyphens and spaces are ignored when decoding.
Copy the result from the output box.

faq.q: How is it different from RFC 4648 Base32?
faq.a: The alphabet and the order differ. Crockford uses 0 to 9 then A to Z without I, L, O and U, while RFC 4648 uses A to Z followed by 2 to 7. Strings are not interchangeable.
No. Padding characters are not used. The last group is filled with zero bits to reach five, so lengths follow directly from the byte count.

faq.q: Does it support the check symbol?
faq.a: No. Crockford describes an optional check character at the end of a value, but this tool encodes and decodes only the data itself, without any check symbol.

faq.q: Is a ULID decoded correctly here?
faq.a: The alphabet matches, but a ULID packs 128 bits into 26 characters with a leading padding, so use the ULID tool to read its timestamp and random part.
